title: Game theory for strategists
note: Game theory studies choices whose results depend on what others choose. Its key tools: the Nash equilibrium (no player gains by changing alone), the prisoner's dilemma (individually rational moves leave both worse off), commitment (binding yourself to change a rival's incentives) and focal points (obvious solutions people coordinate on without talking).

read.title: Thinking one move ahead of the other side
text: A game, in game theory, is any situation where your best choice depends on what others choose. Generals, firms, negotiators and nations all play games in this sense. The central idea is the Nash equilibrium: a set of strategies in which no player could do better by changing course alone, given what the others are doing.

The prisoner's dilemma shows how equilibrium can be bad for everyone. Two suspects are questioned separately. Whatever the other does, each does better by confessing, so both confess, and both end up worse off than if both had stayed silent. Arms races and price wars have the same shape. When the game repeats, though, cooperation can survive, because defection today invites punishment tomorrow.

Thomas Schelling showed that strategy is often bargaining, not just fighting. A threat works only if it is credible, and it is credible only if carrying it out would be in your interest. So a player may deliberately limit his own options, burning his bridges, to make a threat or promise believable. Schelling also noticed that people can coordinate without talking by picking a focal point, an option that stands out to everyone, such as meeting at the main landmark at noon.

q.q: Why do both suspects confess in the prisoner's dilemma?
o: Confessing is better for each whatever the other does

q.q: When can cooperation survive, according to the reading?
o: When one player is much stronger
When the game repeats, so defection invites punishment
When the stakes are very high

q.q: Why might a player deliberately limit his own options?
o: To make a threat or promise credible
